channel.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
channel.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.

item.title: Falcon 9 Block 5 | CHORUS
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of Falcon 9 Block 5, operated by SpaceX. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: CHORUS is MDA's next generation Earth observation constellation, consisting of 2 radar satellites (C-band SAR and X-band SAR), in a 53.5 degree 600 km altitude LEO, with the X-band trailing the C-band by 60 minutes. A collaborative multi-sensor constellation, CHORUS will bring together diverse and unique imagery and data sources and provide a new level of near real-time insight and innovative Earth observation services. Operating in a unique mid-inclination orbit, CHORUS will be able to image day or night, regardless of weather conditions, with daily access of up to 95% of the coverage area. From an industry-leading 700km-wide imaging swath down to sub-metre high resolution, CHORUS will provide the most extensive and unrivalled Earth observation radar imaging capacity available on the market in a single mission. Launch dates slip often – check the current status before tuning into a webcast.

Mission details

item.title: Asteroid 2004 TP1 passes by
item.description:
01.11.2026, 02:13 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 193–431 m will pass Earth at 9.30 million km, or 24.2 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 12.7 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a small hill. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. NASA classifies it as “potentially hazardous” – but that is purely a technical category for objects larger than about 140 m whose orbits come close to Earth's. No known object threatens us in the foreseeable future.

item.title: New Glenn | Blue Ring-1
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of New Glenn, operated by Blue Origin. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: The first mission of Blue Ring, Blue Origin's all-in-one, high-powered hybrid solar electric and chemical propelled spacecraft, will test the spacecraft's operations in Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO), as well as subsequent operations after reaching Geostationary Orbit (GEO). It will carry one of Scout Space's flagship next-generation space domain awareness (SDA) Owl sensors, which is designed to enhance real-time tracking, characterization, and assessment of space objects by integrating advanced optical sensing, onboard artificial intelligence-driven processing, and autonomous decision-making capabilities to deliver domain-wide intelligence in space in support of the U.S. Space Force’s space control mission set. Blue Ring will also carry Optimum Technologies (OpTech)'s next-generation Caracal optical payload, which is designed to provide actionable insights on resident space objects and orbital activity and includes onboard image storage, object detection algorithms, and passive thermal control. The payload is designed to operate flexibly across dynamic orbits over a year-long mission profile. Several internal Blue Origin payloads will also be hosted. item.description:

Launch of Falcon 9 Block 5, operated by SpaceX. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: AST SpaceMobile’s Block 2 BlueBird satellites are designed to deliver up to 10 times the bandwidth capacity of the BlueBird Block 1 satellites, required to achieve 24/7 continuous cellular broadband service coverage in the United States, with beams designed to support a capacity of up to 40 MHz, enabling peak data transmission speeds up to 120 Mbps, supporting voice, full data and video applications. The Block 2 BlueBirds, featuring as large as 2400 square foot communications arrays, will be the largest satellites ever commercially deployed in Low Earth orbit once launched. item.title: Leonids meteor shower peak
item.description:
17.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

A shower that roughly every 33 years erupts into a storm with thousands of meteors an hour. In ordinary years it is quiet. At maximum, up to 15 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Leo. Unfortunately the Moon will be 89% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Greatest western elongation of Mercury (19°)
item.description:
04.11.2027, 08:45 UTC

Mercury stands 19° from the Sun – the best chance this season to catch the planet in the morning, just before sunrise. The hardest planet to catch – it never strays far from the Sun. Look for it low above the eastern horizon during twilight.

item.description:

At maximum, up to 5 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Taurus. A Moon 38% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
